title: Design Patterns: Structural (Adapter, Decorator, Facade, Composite, Proxy)
relevance: High — LLD / machine-coding rounds constantly probe “which wrapper?”, composition vs inheritance, and distinguishing Adapter vs Decorator vs Proxy vs Facade (campus + experienced; FAANG + Indian product cos).
company_notes: Campus / machine coding: Decorator (pizza/coffee/IO), Adapter (multi-provider payment), Composite (file system / org), Facade (library or checkout orchestration) are staples and appear inside parking-lot / bookstore / notification designs. Experienced LLD: Proxy (cache, lazy DAO, auth), Adapter (vendor integrations), and composition-over-inheritance deep dives; interviewers often ask you to contrast two wrappers on the whiteboard. Among the highest-yield LLD fundamentals after SOLID; expect at least one structural pattern by name or by “add feature without changing class X” wording in most product-company LLD rounds.

phases.goal: Establish that structural patterns assemble objects via composition and that the four wrappers differ by interface change vs control vs simplification.

must_hit.point: Structural patterns compose classes/objects into larger structures without inheritance trees that explode; the default tool is composition + delegation behind a shared interface.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Says composition/delegation over exploding inheritance and mentions a shared interface.

must_hit.point: Wrapper distinction: Adapter changes to a different interface; Decorator keeps the same/enhanced interface and adds behavior the client stacks; Proxy keeps the same interface and gates/controls access (often manages the real object); Facade invents a new coarse API over many objects, not a 1:1 stand-in.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Correctly assigns different vs same interface, add-behavior vs control-access, and Facade as subsystem API.

must_hit.point: Decorator vs Composite: both recurse, but Decorator has one child and adds responsibility while Composite has many children and sums/aggregates.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Contrasts one-child add-behavior with many-child aggregate without mixing the two.

probes: What problem do structural patterns solve, and how do you tell Adapter, Decorator, Proxy, and Facade apart in an interview?

hints.1: Start from composition behind a shared interface, then ask whether the interface changes.
hints.2: Map each wrapper: different interface; same interface + add behavior; same interface + control access; new coarse API over a subsystem.
hints.3: Adapter = different interface; Decorator = same + stack behavior; Proxy = same + gate/lifecycle; Facade = new simplified API over many objects.

phases.goal: Show how Adapter, Decorator, Facade, Composite, and Proxy are structured and what each owns.

must_hit.point: Adapter converts an incompatible interface into the one the client already uses (legacy SDK, third-party payment); prefer an object adapter that wraps the adaptee in Java/C#.
must_hit.evidence_hint: States interface translation and prefers wrapping the adaptee over a class-adapter story.

must_hit.point: Decorator wraps an object that already has the same interface to add behavior (logging, compression, toppings) with recursive stacking and client-controlled wrap order; Proxy is a same-interface stand-in that controls access (lazy init, auth, cache, remote, logging) and often owns the real subject’s lifecycle, which Decorator usually does not.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Separates client-stacked add-behavior from access control and who owns the real object.

must_hit.point: Facade exposes one simplified entry point over a noisy subsystem whose classes usually don’t know the facade; Composite models a part–whole tree so clients call the same ops on leaves and containers, with composites recursing and aggregating.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Describes one method over many collaborators for Facade and leaf/container shared interface for Composite.

probes: Walk through Adapter, Decorator, Proxy, Facade, and Composite—what each wraps, whether the interface stays the same, and who owns the real object.

hints.1: For each pattern, say whether the client’s interface changes and whether there is one object or a subsystem.
hints.2: Adapter translates; Decorator stacks same-interface behavior; Proxy gates/lifecycle; Facade simplifies many; Composite shares ops across a tree.
hints.3: Object adapter wraps adaptee; Decorator stacks same interface; Proxy controls access and often owns the subject; Facade is a coarse API over a subsystem; Composite is leaf+container with recursive ops.

phases.goal: Judge when wrappers help versus when they become god classes, ISP tension, or unreadable stacks.

must_hit.point: Don’t introduce Adapter if you can change the source; don’t grow Facade into a god class; don’t Proxy/Decorate everything—wrapper depth hurts debugability and creates order-sensitive bugs.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Refuses unnecessary wrappers and calls out god-facade and deep-stack costs.

must_hit.point: OCP/SRP angle: each adapter/decorator/proxy is a small class so you can add a new payment provider or topping without editing checkout / coffee / IO core.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Ties small wrapper classes to extending without modifying the core path.

must_hit.point: Composite ISP tension: putting add/remove on the Component interface gives a uniform client but empty ops on leaves; keeping them only on Composite is ISP-clean but forces clients to distinguish leaf vs container—pick one and stay consistent.
must_hit.evidence_hint: States both options and a clear preference with the uniformity-vs-ISP tradeoff.

probes: When would you refuse Adapter, Facade, or a Decorator/Proxy stack, and where do you put Composite add/remove?

hints.1: Ask whether the source can change, whether the facade is still a happy-path entry, and how deep the wrappers are.
hints.2: Small wrappers buy OCP; god facades and deep stacks lose; Composite add/remove is uniformity versus ISP.
hints.3: Skip Adapter if source is editable; split unbounded facades; avoid wrapping everything; choose Component-wide or Composite-only child ops and be consistent.

phases.goal: Map structural patterns onto the naming drills, sketches, and code-review prompts interviewers use.

must_hit.point: Name-the-pattern drill: wrap Stripe to fit PaymentProcessor → Adapter; checkout talking to inventory + payment + notify → Facade; milk/sugar on coffee at runtime → Decorator; Folder.getSize over nested files → Composite; load heavy image on first display → Proxy; deny delete unless ADMIN → Proxy.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Assigns each prompt to one pattern and briefly says why not a neighbor wrapper.

must_hit.point: Sketch/IO drills: Adapter LegacyGateway → PaymentProcessor; Decorator stack FileDataSource + Compression + Encryption (order matters); VideoConverter Facade; File/Folder Composite; ImageProxy virtual proxy; explain BufferedInputStream wrapping FileInputStream as Decorator and contrast what Adapter vs Proxy would mean for the same stream.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Draws Client → Interface → Wrapper → Real and can explain Java IO as Decorator with Adapter/Proxy contrast.

must_hit.point: Code-review drill: wrapping UserService for caching and auth may be Proxy, Decorator, or both stacked—argue intent and who creates/owns the real service; also explain why encrypt-then-compress vs compress-then-encrypt changes Decorator stack behavior and how you’d document/test order.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Separates control/lifecycle from optional stacked behavior and calls out wrap-order testing.

probes: For Stripe-to-PaymentProcessor, checkout orchestration, coffee toppings, Folder.getSize, lazy image load, and ADMIN-gated delete—which pattern fits each, and how would you sketch or review the wrappers?

hints.1: Ask whether the interface changes, whether you’re simplifying many objects, adding behavior, or controlling access.
hints.2: Adapter for SDK fit; Facade for multi-collaborator checkout; Decorator for toppings/IO stacks; Composite for tree size; Proxy for lazy load and auth.
hints.3: Stripe→PaymentProcessor = Adapter; checkout orchestration = Facade; milk/sugar = Decorator; Folder.getSize = Composite; lazy image / ADMIN delete = Proxy; then argue ownership and wrap order on review.

tradeoffs.strong_answer: Adapter makes one existing incompatible interface usable by translating it to what the client already expects. Facade invents a new coarse API over a subsystem of many classes so clients call one entry point instead of orchestrating collaborators. Adapter is 1:1 interface translation; Facade is simplification over many objects.

Inheritance is static and combinatorial (BoldItalicUnderline… class explosion). Decorator composes features at runtime behind the same interface so clients stack wrappers without modifying the core class (OCP).

They can look identical in UML (both wrap + delegate). Intent differs: Proxy controls access and often owns the real subject’s lifecycle; Decorator adds optional behavior stacked by the client and usually does not own that lifecycle. A UserService wrap for caching and auth may be Proxy, Decorator, or both stacked—say who creates the real service.

Both recurse. Decorator has one child and adds responsibility; Composite has many children and sums/aggregates (price, draw, size). Don’t treat a topping stack as a part–whole tree or a folder tree as a behavior stack.

Facade is fine as a short happy-path entry over a subsystem whose classes usually don’t know it. If it grows unbounded, split into focused facades (e.g. OrderFacade, PaymentFacade) and keep the common path short rather than absorbing every subsystem detail.

tradeoffs.topic: Composite child ops on Component vs Composite-only
tradeoffs.strong_answer: add/remove on Component gives a uniform client API but leaves empty or throwing ops on leaves. Keeping child ops only on Composite is ISP-cleaner but forces clients to distinguish types. Pick throw, no-op, or Composite-only and stay consistent for leaf safety.

gotchas.trap: Calling Adapter and Facade the same because both ‘wrap’ things
gotchas.correction: Adapter translates one incompatible interface into the client’s expected one. Facade invents a new coarse API over a whole subsystem.

gotchas.trap: Preferring inheritance for optional features like Bold/Italic/Underline
gotchas.correction: Inheritance is static and combinatorial; Decorator stacks those features at runtime without class explosion (OCP).

gotchas.trap: Assuming Proxy and Decorator are different because the UML looks different
gotchas.correction: UML can look identical (wrap + delegate). Distinguish by intent: control access/lifecycle vs optional client-stacked behavior.

gotchas.trap: Treating any Facade as a god class (or letting it become one)
gotchas.correction: A focused happy-path entry is fine; if it grows unbounded, split into focused facades like OrderFacade and PaymentFacade.

gotchas.trap: Calling add on a Composite leaf without a stated policy
gotchas.correction: Choose throw, no-op, or keep child ops only on Composite—and be consistent so leaf safety is clear.

gotchas.trap: Thinking dynamic proxies are unrelated to the Proxy pattern
gotchas.correction: java.lang.reflect.Proxy and Spring AOP are Proxy-family: they intercept calls for transactions, logging, or security without hand-writing each wrapper class.
